item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are set to begin a three-game series against the Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field at 7:10 p.m. EDT on Friday.
Before Friday’s game, the Red Sox announced a notable lineup decision involving outfielder Jarren Duran.
Boston Red Sox Announce Jarren Duran Decision Before Rays Series
Duran is out of the Red Sox’s lineup for Friday’s game. He started in center field in Thursday’s 5-4 win over the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas.
The Rays are starting left-hander Ian Seymour on the mound, which is likely why manager Chad Tracy elected to sit Duran, a left-handed hitter.
Here is the Red Sox’s full lineup for Friday:
- Roman Anthony LF
- Nick Sogard 1B
- Jahmai Jones DH
- Wilyer Abreu RF
- Trevor Story SS
- Caleb Durbin 3B
- Isiah Kiner-Falefa 2B
- Nate Eaton CF
- Connor Wong C
Starting Pitcher: LHP Ranger Suarez (7-4, 3.33 ERA, 130 K)
Here is the Rays’ lineup:
- Yainer Diaz DH
- Jonathan Aranda 1B
- Junior Caminero 3B
- Ryan Vilade 2B
- Chandler Simpson LF
- Jonny DeLuca CF
- Nick Fortes C
- Victor Mesa Jr. RF
- Taylor Walls SS
Starting Pitcher: LHP Ian Seymour (9-6, 4.27 ERA, 150 K)
Looking at Jarren Duran
Duran has had a rough season, posting just 0.2 bWAR and a .203/.259/.359 slash line with 20 home runs and 69 RBI over 143 games.
Just two seasons ago, Duran posted 9.0 bWAR and an .834 OPS with 21 home runs and 75 RBI. He had a solid 2025 season as well, posting 4.9 bWAR and a 114 OPS+.
Duran has especially struggled this month, hitting just .159/.213/.250 in 44 at-bats.
On the bright side, Duran has been a spectacular defender for Boston this year, posting +5 Outs Above Average.
Boston Red Sox Right Now
Before beating the Rangers on Thursday, the Red Sox lost the first two games of the series against Texas. Boston is 5-5 in its last 10 games.
At this point in the season, Boston seems locked in to the second AL Wild Card spot unless something crazy happens. If the standings hold up, the Red Sox will play the New York Yankees in the Wild Card round at Yankee Stadium.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Trevor Story’s late home run helps Red Sox flip script on Rangers

item.content:encoded:
This has been a rough stretch for the Red Sox offense, which has effectively turned into a pumpkin after a torrid two months this summer. This week in particular the bats have fallen silent, and for much of Thursday night the Red Sox looked like they were headed toward a discouraging series sweep at the worst possible time.
Things took an especially grim turn when Willson Contreras left the game in the eighth inning after being hit in the hand by a pitch, but while the specter of his absence will loom over the club in the days to come, Trevor Story once again proved that you can never count this Red Sox team out.
The veteran shortstop came through with a go-ahead three-run home run in the top of the eighth inning, flipping the script and giving the Red Sox a badly needed 4-3 win to avoid a sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers.
Story’s shot came with one out against Rangers closer Jacob Latz, completing a three-run comeback and cutting Boston’s magic number to clinch a playoff spot to three with nine games remaining.
“To steal that last one is huge,” Story told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “It’s momentum we can ride out into Tampa.”
Prior to Story’s home run, Thursday was shaping up to be among the club’s worst losses of the season.
A hallmark of the offense’s struggles early in the year was a lot of empty, uncompetitive at-bats, tons of swing and miss and a general inability to make good contact. Even with the Rangers opting for a bullpen game led by Cody Bradford, whose fastball averages just 88.6 mph, the Red Sox couldn’t square anything up.
The Red Sox only managed two hits through the first five innings, both singles in the fourth inning. That put runners at the corners with two outs, but Jarren Duran grounded out to squander the opportunity.
It was a similar story in the sixth, when Wilyer Abreu singled and Adley Rutschman finally did some damage with a ground-rule double into the left-field gap. Had the ball stayed in play, Abreu probably would have scored, but instead the Red Sox had two men in scoring position for Story, who worked a full count and struck out to end the threat.
The offense did nothing to pick up Sonny Gray, who wasn’t perfect but did everything he could to keep the Red Sox in the game.
The veteran right-hander allowed a solo home run to Josh Jung with two outs in the first, and in the second he walked the first two batters of the inning, both of whom came around to score on an RBI bloop single by Danny Jansen and a run-scoring squeeze bunt by Evan Carter.
Gray settled down afterward and retired 14 of the last 16 batters he faced from the second inning into the seventh. He was charged with three runs over 6 1/3 innings and limited the Rangers to three hits and three walks with six strikeouts.
“I thought he was awesome,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said. “The only blemish was the two walks, we kind of walked ourselves into the part of their lineup where they can play baseball a little bit with bunts and they drop a flare into center and there’s a safety squeeze, outside of that, that was a really, really good effort.”
Even when the Red Sox finally scored in the top of the seventh, they did so without recording a hit. Nate Eaton and Caleb Durbin led off with consecutive walks and Eaton advanced to third after Nick Sogard hit a rocket of a fly out to the center field wall. But with one out and a chance to fight back into the game, Roman Anthony grounded into a run-scoring fielder’s choice to make it 3-1. He advanced to second after the Rangers threw away the double-play attempt, but Mickey Gasper grounded out to end the inning.
Then came the eighth.
Once again the Red Sox got two men on base right away, with Abreu drawing a leadoff walk before Contreras was hit in the right hand by a pitch. He immediately left the game with the trainer and was replaced at first by Isiah Kiner-Falefa, but while the Red Sox worried about their slugger, the Rangers pulled Jakob Junis for their closer Latz, who has been among the most dominant closers in the American League this year.
Latz drew a pop out from Rutschman, but then Story stepped up to the plate and everything changed.
“You see one of our guys keeled over holding his hand and you’re down in the dumps seeing that and moments later the whole dugout erupts,” Tracy said. “We haven’t been doing much offensively for a few days and to get a swing right there and feel like you steal a game, it was enormous. Big emotion swing.”
With the lead in hand, Wyatt Olds and Alec Gamboa pitched a scoreless eighth, and with Aroldis Chapman unavailable, Garrett Whitlock came on for the ninth and locked down the save for the win. Story and Sogard turned inning-ending double plays in both the eighth and the ninth to ensure the Rangers couldn’t mount one last comeback.
“Good teams find a way to win and we’ve been doing that in the second half and that’s kind of who you become,” Story said. “And you feel that momentum, you feel that vibe around the game and we never give up.”
X-rays negative, Chapman day-to-day
The Red Sox got some good news postgame when X-rays on Contreras’ hand came back negative.
“He’s got a bruise on the hand and some swelling,” Tracy said. “So we’ll just take it day to day and see how he is.”
Tracy also confirmed that Chapman has been dealing with some lat tightness for the past few days and they are taking a conservative approach.
“It’s getting better but have to make sure it gets there, that’s why he wasn’t available tonight,” Tracy said, adding that an IL stint isn’t being considered for Chapman right now.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox need something to change Thursday night. Putting Jarren Duran back in the lineup is a start.
Boston will turn to Duran in center field for Thursday's series finale against the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field after he did not start Wednesday's 7-3 loss. The Red Sox have dropped the first two games of the series and enter Thursday at 82-70 with only 10 games remaining in the regular season.
Roman Anthony will remain in the leadoff spot and start in left field, while Jahmai Jones gets another opportunity at designated hitter. Wilyer Abreu, Willson Contreras and Adley Rutschman make up the middle of the order.
Christopher Smith of MassLive shared Boston's lineup shortly after it was released Thursday.
The complete Red Sox lineup:
- Roman Anthony, LF
- Jahmai Jones, DH
- Wilyer Abreu, RF
- Willson Contreras, 1B
- Adley Rutschman, C
- Trevor Story, SS
- Jarren Duran, CF
- Caleb Durbin, 3B
- Nick Sogard, 2B
Sonny Gray will start on the mound.
Red Sox bring Duran back for crucial series finale
Duran's return is one of the most notable changes from Wednesday's lineup. The 30-year-old was not in the starting nine Wednesday, when Boston used Nate Eaton in center field and Isiah Kiner-Falefa at second base.
Red Sox lineup: Anthony LF, Jones DH, Abreu RF, Contreras 1B, Rutschman C, Story SS, Duran LF, Durbin 3B, Sogard 2B, Gray P
— Christopher Smith (@SmittyOnMLB) September 17, 2026
Neither is starting Thursday.
Instead, Duran returns to center, Sogard takes over at second and Trevor Story moves up one spot in the order to hit sixth.
Boston could certainly use a spark.
The Red Sox entered Texas with an opportunity to strengthen their postseason position but instead have lost consecutive games to a Rangers team fighting for its own playoff life. Texas improved to 76-76 with Wednesday's victory and has won four consecutive games. The Rangers are only one game behind the Chicago White Sox for the final American League wild-card spot.
Boston remains in much better shape, holding the second AL wild card with a five-game cushion over Chicago entering Thursday. That cushion is significant. It isn't comfortable enough to keep losing.
The Red Sox have gone 5-5 over their last 10 games, and Thursday represents their final opportunity to leave Texas with something positive before the schedule moves into its final nine games.
Sonny Gray gets the ball with Red Sox needing a win
If there is a pitcher Boston would want on the mound in this situation, Gray makes a compelling case. The veteran right-hander enters Thursday with a 17-5 record and 2.76 ERA.
Texas will counter with left-hander Tyler Alexander, who enters at 5-2 with a 3.38 ERA. The left-handed starter helps explain some of Boston's lineup decisions.
Jones, a right-handed hitter, remains in the No. 2 spot after starting there Wednesday. Contreras gives Boston another right-handed bat in the cleanup position, while Rutschman follows him from the fifth spot.
Anthony remains atop everything.
Boston has continued trusting the rookie in the leadoff role during the most important stretch of the season, and that won't change with a left-hander on the mound Thursday.
The larger question is whether the Red Sox can finally turn opportunities into enough runs.
Boston's postseason position remains favorable, but the Rangers have provided a reminder of how quickly September can become uncomfortable.
A sweep would send the Red Sox into the final nine games on a three-game losing streak. A win would allow them to leave Texas with their playoff cushion intact and Gray having stopped the bleeding. With Duran back in the lineup, Boston is hoping Thursday looks considerably different from the first two nights of the series. First pitch from Globe Life Field is scheduled for 8:05 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are still sitting comfortably in the second Wild Card spot, but there are several issues they must resolve before they start thinking about playoff baseball.
Boston is a mediocre 11-11 over its last 22 games. While that's been good enough to sustain its playoff position, its play hasn't exactly inspired optimism for a deep postseason run.
Most of the Red Sox' problems can be linked to their underperforming lineup. Key hitters like Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Wilyer Abreu have been concerningly inconsistent.
A deeper dive into the numbers suggests the struggling Sox will have their work cut out for them in their presumed Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium. Here are the club's five biggest areas of concern with 10 games remaining:
Roman Anthony is ice-cold
The Red Sox need Roman Anthony to be one of their best offensive players to have any chance of a deep postseason run. If the former No. 1 prospect continues to play the way he has for most of September, that will be problematic.
Anthony is hitting just .149 (7-for-47) with one home run and a .428 OPS over his last 11 games. He has struck out 18 times in 51 plate appearances.
The 22-year-old's struggles beg the question: should he still be the leadoff hitter in the postseason? Interim manager Chad Tracy will have no choice but to reevaluate Anthony's spot in the lineup if his woes continue. The problem with that is there aren't any exciting alternatives. The leadoff spot has been a glaring issue all season long, regardless of who has been thrust into the role.
Struggling against high velocity
The Red Sox offense has been inconsistent no matter who's on the mound, but it has mostly struggled against pitchers with high velo. Here's how some of Boston's regulars have fared this season against pitches greater than or equal to 97 mph:
- Wilyer Abreu: .170 BA, .623 OPS (237 pitches)
- Jarren Duran: .065 BA, .300 OPS (203 pitches)
- Willson Contreras: .170 BA, .512 OPS (166 pitches)
- Ceddanne Rafaela: .205 BA, .449 OPS (157 pitches)
- Roman Anthony: .091 BA, .440 OPS (58 pitches)
- Adley Rutschman: .077 BA, .451 OPS (57 pitches)
The Red Sox' top performer against high velocity (97 mph and above) has been Caleb Durbin (.364 BA, .912 OPS, 161 pitches).
Being so vulnerable against high velocity will especially be a problem for Boston in its expected Wild Card Series matchup against the New York Yankees. Cy Young frontrunner and likely Game 1 starter Cam Schlittler averages 98 mph with his four-seam fastball, which he uses 44.5 percent of the time. Gerrit Cole averages 96.9 mph with his four-seam, using it 49.3 percent of the time.
Leaving runners stranded
Boston has been below average all season at capitalizing on runners in scoring position. It currently ranks 17th in batting average (.250) and 21st in OPS (.731) with RISP. They're hitting just .212 in such situations through 14 games so far in September.
The Yankees' elite pitching staff probably won't provide the Red Sox with many scoring opportunities in their short series, so it's imperative that they come through when given the chance. Lately, Boston hasn't had anyone in its lineup to feel confident about when they step to the plate with runners on.
Role players regressing
As great as guys like Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and Wilyer Abreu were throughout the Red Sox' incredible midseason turnaround, it was the role players who powered their surge. Mickey Gasper, Jahmai Jones, Nick Sogard, Anthony Seigler, and Andruw Monasterio were instrumental in resurrecting Boston's season.
Gasper has cooled off, though no one expected him to sustain his Barry Bonds-like run. Jahmai Jones is 4 for his last 22 (.182) with nine strikeouts, suddenly making him a playoff roster cut candidate. Sogard is still hitting, but his .758 OPS so far in September suggests regression to the mean. Seigler is hurt. Monasterio posted a .578 OPS in August and is 0-for-11 so far in September, putting him on the playoff roster bubble.
That group deserves immense credit for getting the Red Sox here, but it cannot be counted on to propel the club through the postseason.
Erik Miller experiencing command issues
Boston's bullpen is arguably its biggest strength heading into the postseason. The back end with Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Aroldis Chapman is elite.
We would've included trade deadline addition Erik Miller in that group last month, when he allowed only one earned run with 20 strikeouts and just three walks across his first 11 appearances with the Red Sox. His performance so far this month, however, has been alarming.
Miller, acquired from the San Francisco Giants in the Marcelo Mayer trade, has allowed four earned runs with six walks and six strikeouts through five appearances (4.1 IP) in September. His command struggles were a question mark upon his joining the club, and it appears that issue has reemerged with less than two weeks until the playoffs.
After Wednesday's poor outing against the Texas Rangers (2 H, 3 ER, 1 BB), Miller attributed his recent struggles to his mechanics. The Red Sox will hope that whatever the problem is, it's a quick fix, because Miller will be counted on to be their most reliable left-handed reliever not named Aroldis Chapman.

item.content:encoded:
After a historic run in late June and into July, you knew things would end up evening out for the Boston Red Sox. That appears to be the case in September. With 10 games remaining in the regular season, the Red Sox are five games clear of the third and final American League wild-card spot.
They are destined for a matchup in a couple of weeks in a best-of-three series against the New York Yankees in the Bronx. However, Boston is struggling as the regular season winds down after a 7-3 loss to the Texas Rangers on Wednesday night in Arlington. The Red Sox are 5-5 in their last 10 games. What's going on in September? Interim manager Chad Tracy had a simple answer.
Boston Red Sox Interim Manager Chad Tracy Drops Simple Answer on Team's Struggles
Boston is 0-2 on their final road trip of the regular season and will look to avoid a sweep by Texas on Thursday night. They will be sending ace Sonny Gray to the mound. However, the loss on Wednesday night was another frustrating one, but Tracy had a simple answer for his teams recent struggles.
"Probably the easy answer is: baseball," Tracy said, per Tim Healey of the Boston Globe. "We got some guys going through it, and then you could see one or two big swings in a complete turn the other direction. So we just gotta keep plugging away at it."
First baseman Willson Contreras gave Boston a 2-0 first-inning lead on a two-run home run. However, Texas scored seven of the game's final eight runs. Contreras said that despite the recent stretch, Boston is in the right mind set.
"First-inning homer, it's always good, but it's even better if we win," Contreras said, per Healey. "We battle. We come here with the right mindset. We work hard . . . But sometimes it's baseball. Sometimes, it doesn't matter how hard we work. Sometimes, the results are not gonna come. But you have to build off that. You have to take those types of games personal and get better for tomorrow."
Boston managed just two hits over the last eight innings. Trevor Story and pinch-hitter Nick Sogard had the other two hits. That won't win many regular season games, never mind playoff games.
Boston Red Sox Have Difficult Regular Season Schedule Left
Boston's 10 remaining games are all against teams with something to play for. Texas is tied for the AL West lead with the Houston Astros. The Rays are looking to fend off the Yankees to win the AL East.
Their final two series at home are against the Cleveland Guardians and Chicago Cubs. The Guardians are battling the Chicago White Sox for the AL Central Division. Whoever wins the division will most likely get a wild-card round bye. If they don't, the AL West winner will. As for the Cubs, they are battling the Philadelphia Phillies for home-field advantage in the National League wild-card round.
Going into the playoffs, teams want to be playing their best baseball. That's not the case right now for the Red Sox. However, there is still time to gain momentum going into the postseason.

item.content:encoded:
The limp to October goes on for the Boston Red Sox, who blew an early 2-0 lead Wednesday night, and dropped the series in Texas with a 7-3 loss that improved the Rangers to 76-76.
Boston batters managed just three hits, their runs coming via Willson Contreras’ first-inning two-run homer and Caleb Durbin scoring on a balk in the fifth.
Early on, it looked like both starting pitchers were not going to last long.
Rangers lefty MacKenzie Gore began Wednesday’s game with a four-pitch walk, three of which were nowhere near the zone, to Red Sox leadoff man Roman Anthony, and gave up Contreras’ team-leading 27th homer.
Sox rookie southpaw Jake Bennett labored through a 26-pitch bottom of the first in which he faced six batters and gave up a run.
But after a second-inning delay in which it seemed like Gore was about to depart, he completed four innings. Bennett went 4 2/3. Both starters allowed three earned runs, though Gore only yielded two hits to Bennett’s eight.
“Overall, not horrible,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters of Bennett. “The first inning they were able to make him throw some pitches, so the pitches stacked up on him. But at the end of the day, he left with the lead, was competitive. … Usually you’re accustomed to see him pitching deeper, but they were pesky with their at-bats, fouled a lot of stuff off, and drove the count up.”
The Red Sox retook the lead on Jakob Junis’ fifth-inning balk. It evaporated for good one pitch into Greg Weissert’s appearance when he took over for Bennett in the bottom of the inning.
Erik Miller’s three-run blowup seventh inning was the unnecessary coup de grâce for a Red Sox team struggling to so much as collect a hit, much less score a run. But it marked Miller’s worst outing of the season, with Boston or San Francisco, and his third time allowing runs in his last six appearances.
“Just not doing what I’ve been doing well, just not getting ahead of guys, falling behind counts, getting into hitters counts,” a subdued Miller told reporters postgame. “I mean, doesn’t really matter how good your stuff is; guy knows what’s coming, it usually doesn’t end as well.”
“Just kind of working through some stuff right now,” Miller continued. “There’s some stuff (I’m) trying to clean up a little bit on the mechanical side. … At some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. And I’d been doing really well, and some bad habits kind of fallen back into. So yeah, just got to work through it, kind of get back to what I was doing, and go from there.”
2018 World Series hero Nathan Eovaldi closed out the win with four shutout innings against his former team. It marked the veteran righty’s first relief appearance since 2020: Game 4 of the 2021 ALCS with the Red Sox.
To add insult to the injury of Boston’s decision not to re-sign Eovaldi following the 2022 season, his 46 wins since 2023 are tied for second-most among all American League pitchers in that span.
Trevor Story’s infield single in the fifth and Nick Sogard’s pinch-hit single in the sixth comprised the rest of Boston’s hits. The lineup managed three walks and struck out three times in the contest. They were 0 for 7 with runners in scoring position, and left three men on base.
“Yeah, we’re going through it a little bit,” Tracy said of his lineup. “We didn’t have a ton, we didn’t create a ton of opportunities.”
Game highlights were few and far between for the Red Sox. The short list included the usual elite defense from right fielder Wilyer Abreu, who is all but guaranteed to win his third consecutive Gold Glove Award, and continued displays of ABS expertise by new catcher Adley Rutschman, who went 3 for 3 in challenges.
The Red Sox have lost five of their last seven games since their five-game win streak. They are 7-7 in September, 10-11 in their last 20 games, and 82-70 overall.
Their magic number to clinch a postseason spot is five. But there is little magic lately.

item.content:encoded:
Since returning from injury on August 30, Roman Anthony has looked more like the 2025 version of himself than he did at the beginning of the season. He's hitting .258 with a .764 OPS. In his 15 games, he's got five RBI and six extra-base hits; it's good for a 109 WRC+. It's exactly what the Red Sox needed from him in his return from his May 4 injury.
The one thing Anthony has struggled with has been leading off the game. He has hit leadoff in every game he's played since his return and has only two singles, a double, and five strikeouts with no walks in that spot. It's probably time to have someone else lead off.
In his absence (May 5-August 29), Red Sox leadoff hitters had success in the first inning. While they only hit .213, they had a .307 on-base percentage and a .449 slugging percentage, which equated to a 108 WRC+. Surprisingly, most of that success came from Jarren Duran, who hit leadoff 31 of the 101 games and had a 141 WRC+.
Roman Anthony hasn't performed in the first inning, but he has the rest of the game
Anthony has struggled in the leadoff spot all season. In a total of 36 games, the lefty has a .299 OPS in the first inning. In the second inning or later this season, Anthony boasts a .280/.395/.439/.834 slash line and a 136 WRC+. In those same innings, in only the games he was first in the batting order, he has a .792 OPS and 125 WRC+.
Something about him batting first in the first inning isn't working for him. Whether it's his approach or the way pitchers are attacking him in that spot, Anthony hasn't been able to put it together this season. That's why it's time to drop him down in the order.
That doesn't mean to all of a sudden move him down to seventh in the order, but to push him down to second or third and put a player with high on-base skills in front of him. The Sox have had a few players show really great on-base skills this season. Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, and Isiah Kiner-Falefa are all players with an OBP over .340 this season. Having one of them leadoff, then getting on base in front of Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela, Willson Contreras, and Wilyer Abreu would be extremely dangerous.
Anthony hasn't shown he can hack it leading off the game this season; it's been his one real weak point since his return. With two weeks until the start of the playoffs and a postseason berth almost assured (100% per FanGraphs as of September 15th), now is the time to experiment with the lineup and fix this problem before they get to October.

Red Sox Sit Jarren Duran, Shake Up Lineup For Rangers Matchup originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Boston Red Sox will give their lineup a significantly different look Wednesday night as they attempt to respond to a frustrating series-opening loss. Jarren Duran is out of the starting lineup against Texas Rangers left-hander MacKenzie Gore. Mickey Gasper and Nick Sogard also will begin the game on the bench after starting Tuesday's 4-2 defeat at Globe Life Field.
Jahmai Jones will replace Gasper at designated hitter and bat second. Isiah Kiner-Falefa enters at second base, while Nate Eaton will take over for Duran in center field.
Boston officially announced its revamped batting order on X before the second game of the three-game series. Roman Anthony remains in the leadoff spot and will play left field. Wilyer Abreu moves from fifth to third, while Willson Contreras stays in the cleanup spot.
Adley Rutschman drops two places in the order after batting third Tuesday. The catcher will hit fifth, followed by Caleb Durbin, Trevor Story, Kiner-Falefa and Eaton.
Red Sox Lineup Vs. Rangers
- Roman Anthony, LF
- Jahmai Jones, DH
- Wilyer Abreu, RF
- Willson Contreras, 1B
- Adley Rutschman, C
- Caleb Durbin, 3B
- Trevor Story, SS
- Isiah Kiner-Falefa, 2B
- Nate Eaton, CF
Jake Bennett will start on the mound for Boston. The left-hander enters Wednesday with a 9-7 record, a 3.69 ERA and 83 strikeouts. Gore will oppose Bennett for Texas. The Rangers left-hander is 8-11 with a 4.62 ERA and 172 strikeouts.
The matchup with Gore likely contributed to manager Chad Tracy loading the bottom half of his lineup with right-handed hitters. Jones, Contreras, Durbin, Story, Kiner-Falefa and Eaton all will bat from the right side. Boston needs a better collective offensive performance after producing only two runs in Tuesday's opener. Sogard supplied both with a two-run home run against Jacob deGrom in the third inning, but the Red Sox could not complete the comeback after falling behind 4-0.
The loss dropped Boston to 82-69 with only 11 regular-season games remaining. The Red Sox entered Wednesday 9 1/2 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East and 5 1/2 games behind the New York Yankees.
Wednesday's first pitch is scheduled for 8:05 p.m. ET at Globe Life Field. NESN will carry the game.

item.content:encoded:
Ranger Suarez tossed his second straight seven-inning start and the Boston Red Sox scored in their final three at-bats en route to a 5-1 win over the visiting Kansas City Royals on Saturday afternoon.
Suarez (7-4) struck out eight, scattered five hits and allowed one run while completing his seven frames in 96 pitches as Boston (81-68) snapped its three-game losing streak.
Roman Anthony, Adley Rutschman and Nick Sogard each had multiple hits while Wilyer Abreu hit a two-run double that gave the Red Sox a sixth-inning lead they would not relinquish.
Carter Jensen’s 24th home run of the season marked the only scoring for Kansas City (66-83), which opened the series with a win Friday.
The Red Sox took the lead with two runs on three straight hits in the sixth. After Mickey Gasper and Rutschman knocked back-to-back singles to right to chase Royals starter Randy Dobnak (3-4), Abreu drove them home with a two-out double to deep center off reliever Anthony Gose.
The lead grew in each of the next two frames, beginning with Sogard hitting a leadoff double and scoring on Caleb Durbin’s RBI single off the Green Monster in the seventh.
After Garrett Whitlock struck out the side in the Royals’ eighth, Trevor Story and Sogard posted back-to-back doubles to plate another run.
Aroldis Chapman followed with a scoreless ninth to tab Suarez with the victory.
The teams plowed through three scoreless innings with just one baserunner: Bobby Witt Jr.’s one-out single in Kansas City’s opening frame. Suarez stranded him on third after recording back-to-back outs, including an inning-ending strikeout of Vinnie Pasquantino.
Suarez retired the Royals 1-2-3 on 10 pitches in the second and third innings while Dobnak faced the minimum, striking out three batters through the first third of the game.
In the fourth, Anthony turned a leadoff single through the right side into the opening run. After moving to second on Gasper’s grounder, Anthony scored when Rutschman knocked a single into center.
After finishing the fourth around Pasquantino’s two-out double, Suarez retired five straight before Jensen’s one-out solo homer inside Pesky’s Pole in the sixth. The southpaw stranded runners in the next two frames, including back-to-back strikeouts to cap the seventh.
–Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Justin Slaten’s injury: The Red Sox bullpen got a dose of bad news earlier this week when it was learned that reliever Justin Slaten — who has been out since Aug. 16 with what was initially called right elbow inflammation — is now likely to miss the rest of the season.
Interim manager Chad Tracy spoke to reporters about the matter on Tuesday, acknowledging that the injury is worse than what was originally thought. Slaten, 29, saw well respected orthopedic and sports medicine surgeon Keith Meister in Arlington, Texas prior to the team’s series against the Rangers, and was diagnosed with a more problematic issue.
“There’s some degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” Tracy explained, via Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. “So that’s substantially different news.”
Along with an injection of injection of platelet-rich plasma, Slaten will continue to rest. His status for the remainder of the 2026 season, already up in the air, now appears to be settled.
“This maybe adds some finality to the fact,” Tracy said of Slaten being out. “We were already operating that way, but you still held out hope.
“It’s a big loss — at least now, the finality of knowing we can’t have it back,” Tracy concluded.
Slaten had a 4.60 ERA in 31.1 innings in 2026 (36 appearances). His loss will be partly offset by the expected return this week of fellow reliever Tyson Guerrero, who has been on the injured list since Sept 1.
Trivia: What Red Sox pitcher holds the team’s single-season record for appearances?
(Answer at the bottom).
Hint: He did it in 2005 (81 total appearances), and won four World Series titles in his career (two in Boston, two in Toronto).
More from Boston.com:
Out of the ballpark in a hurry: Though it proved to be not enough for a win on Tuesday, Nick Sogard hit a line drive home run that left the yard at high speed.
On this day: On the same day that the struggling Red Sox fired general manager Mike “Pinky” Higgins, Boston right-hander Dave Morehead threw a no-hitter in front of just 1,247 fans at Fenway Park. Morehead’s heroics helped the Red Sox defeat future Boston ace Luis Tiant and Cleveland by a 2-0 final score. It would be the last Red Sox no-hitter until Hideo Nomo in 2001.
Daily highlight: An absolute missile from Liverpool midfielder Dominik Szoboszlai helped ensure a win (3-1) over Tottenham in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday.
Trivia answer: Mike Timlin

item.content:encoded:
BOSTON — In a one-run game against the Kansas City Royals’ last homestand, Boston Red Sox shortstop Trevor Story hit a one-out double off the wall, raced to second base and dove head-first into the bag.
He flipped over on his back and held onto the bag, a safe call upheld after a Royals’ challenge.
Advertisement
The Red Sox eventually lost that game, but it was a small play that represented the bigger picture: Story was back. A diving, flipping play would have been hard to imagine for Story — or anyone watching him — earlier this season as he battled through a sports hernia injury that left him hitting .206 with a .547 OPS after 41 games.
Following surgery in May and a rehab that forced him to miss 93 games this season, Story has made a quiet but impactful return to the team.
He has hit safely in 13 of 14 games since returning, including Tuesday’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers. Since his activation Aug. 30 in New York, Story has started at shortstop in 14 of the team’s 15 games, going 19-for-56 (.339) with seven doubles and six RBIs. He’s hoping to make up for lost time.
“That was, ideally, the point of the surgery, to get it and come back and be able to do the things that I know I can do,” the 33-year-old said.
“It’s not invisible,” he said of the sports hernia’s effects. “I don’t think you would expect it to be after surgery and coming back. But it’s so much better than it was, and I’m getting stronger. So I’m happy about that. And I’m happy with the way my body has reacted. I wanted to be a part of this.”
It’s admittedly a small sample size since Story has returned, but if he had started slowly following his return, the calls for him to be replaced in the lineup would have grown louder. His replacements at shortstop — particularly a combination of Andruw Monasterio and Nick Sogard — filled in admirably during his absence as the Red Sox turned their season around. Story’s unproductive 10 rehab games with Triple-A Worcester, coupled with the rise of top prospect Franklin Arias, a shortstop raking at Triple A, created an echo chamber of angst about Story returning and underperforming.
So far, he hasn’t.
Advertisement
And he’s heard much of the criticism and frustration about his impending return. He understands it. His injury-riddled tenure in Boston has warranted that consternation. He missed much of 2024 recovering from extensive shoulder surgery and 2023 from elbow surgery. Of his five years in Boston, on a six-year, $140 million deal, he’s played only one healthy season.
Staying on the field has been his biggest bugaboo with the Red Sox. But the outside noise and frustration with his injuries motivated Story to prove he can still play.
“You see a lot of that stuff, but I really try to channel it into an energy in a way that I can use,” he said. “At the time, I wasn’t trying to pay much attention to it, but people would bring it to me, and I decided how I was going to look at it. I just tried to channel it into when I do come back, and it’s all about the playoffs, and it’s all about winning this thing at the end. That’s where I put my energy and focus.”
Roman Anthony, who missed 101 games with a torn finger ligament and rehabbed alongside Story, learned by watching the veteran handle the pressure.
“He’s unbelievable,” said Anthony. “Getting to go through this process with him. I was so happy for him. Every at-bat, he just continues to look better and better, and then to trust himself through all the noise.”
The return to the field has taken Story some effort, though. He arrives at the field roughly an hour before the team’s mandatory report time so that he can get on the trainer’s table to be stretched out for 30 to 45 minutes before his activation work in the gym, which leads into the team’s daily hitters’ meeting, then his workout before cage and field work.
“I’ve learned to kind of streamline it a little bit, and with the injury, (I) kind of know what (I) need,” he said. “In the gym, I’m just activating the right muscles, getting the core going, getting the hips right, adductor, glute med, the surrounding muscles from my surgery. So a lot of it is pre-hab. It’s mainly about the hips and getting the rotations right.”
Advertisement
The work has paid off early on. On Aug. 31, his first game back at Fenway Park in nearly four months, he cranked a base hit off the wall in the bottom of the ninth for a walk-off win.
This past Sunday, he padded a slim Red Sox lead against the Royals with a two-run single in the eighth. He’s hoping to carry this production through the rest of the season to prove he can be the player who hit .289 with an .827 OPS over the final four months of the 2025 season.
Despite missing so much of the year, the recent production since has helped him feel a part of the Red Sox’ run.
“As I’m sitting there watching the 15-game winning streak and starting to turn the whole season around, you watch it from the dugout and it’s like, ‘Man, this is something special,'” he said. “To be able to play a part and do my thing this late in the season means a lot to me.”

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — The Red Sox didn’t have many big swings Tuesday night against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers, but one from a late-game pinch-hitter nearly flipped the script on the whole night.
Pinch-hitting for Jarren Duran against All-Star closer Jacob Latz in the eighth inning with Boston trailing by two, Andruw Monasterio got a 3-2 fastball just below the zone and smoked it — just foul. Monasterio sent a screaming line drive down the left field line, but it landed in the seats in foul territory, 369 feet away from home plate. If the ball had landed a few feet to its right, the Red Sox would have led 6-4 heading into the ninth.
For a second, the Red Sox dugout (on the third base side) thought Monasterio was a hero.
“It’s hard to tell from the dugout, from our angle,” said interim manager Chad Tracy. “When it came off the bat, it looked like, ‘Is that gonna hit the foul pole?’ But for about halfway on the ball flight, it was like, ‘I think that might hit the foul pole, I think it might be close.’”
Instead, Monasterio’s at-bat continued and Latz blew a 97 mph fastball by him to escape the threat. It was the second bases-loaded escape for the Rangers, who also didn’t allow a run in a similar situation in the fifth. In all, the Red Sox were hitless in four at-bats with runners in scoring position and left nine on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up,” Tracy said. “We just couldn’t do it tonight.”
The pressure-filled situation marked just Monasterio’s 12th plate appearance in 15 games since Trevor Story and Roman Anthony were both activated from the injured list August 30.
Sandoval struggles
When starter Patrick Sandoval struck out the first four batters of his outing, it looked like he was about to go toe-to-toe with deGrom, the five-time All-Star on the other side. But that illusion quickly collapsed in a brutal second inning in which Sandoval allowed four runs and threw 44 pitches.
Sandoval allowed two separate rallies as the Rangers scored four times with two outs. With two men on after both singled, Elias Díaz opened the scoring with a two-run double to left. Sandoval then walked two batters in a row before Corey Seager plated two runs with a bloop single to left-center.
“Just got to pitch better,” said Sandoval, who has a 4.99 ERA. “Got to do better for this team. Can’t be doing this.”
Sandoval was the victim of some bad luck as Seager’s single left the bat at just 67.2 mph and traveled 212 feet. The ball fell in no man’s land between Story and Anthony and glanced off Story’s glove. Still, Sandoval took the blame.
“Just got to make a better pitch,” Sandoval said. “That’s it.”
Sandoval lasted just 2 ⅔ innings in Boston’s 4-2 loss, allowing four earned runs on four hits while walking two batters. He did have five strikeouts.
Sogard homers again
The only scoring of the night for the Red Sox came in the third when Nick Sogard launched a line-drive two-run shot off deGrom that tucked inside the right field foul pole. Considering Boston had just three hits against deGrom, it was an impressive swing on a slider down and in.
“I’d only gotten one fastball that at-bat and it was kinda up-and-in, so with two strikes, he likes to back-foot it,” Sogard said. “One of the best pitchers in the game. Ton of respect for him. But I had a feeling it was going to be something in. I definitely wasn’t sitting on it. I was a little out in front, but I was able to keep it fair and it got over the wall.”
Sogard waited a while for his first big league homer, going 321 plate appearances before going deep against Arizona on August 19. Including Tuesday, he has now homered five times in his last 99 trips to the plate.
“I feel good,” he said. “Just trying to compete and grind out good at-bats and get your pitches to hit. I’ve been able to drive it a little bit better this year.”
Bullpen strategy keeps options open
When Tracy pulled Sandoval with two outs in the third and Wyatt Langford coming to the plate, he went to righty Brayan Bello, a common piggyback option who has given the Red Sox plenty of long relief appearances and threw 103 pitches in his last outing, a start against the Angels on Labor Day. But Tracy chose to only use Bello for 1 ⅔ innings (and 19 pitches). It was his shortest appearance of the year.
The reason, Tracy said, was to keep the possibility open for Bello to make a longer appearance (potentially a start) later in the week. Boston’s well-rested bullpen cobbled together the rest of the game with Bello (five outs), Alec Gamboa (three), Wyatt Olds (two) and Jovani Morán (six) passing the baton.
“We’re keeping options open,” said Tracy. “Part of the reason we were able to be so aggressive is that so much of the bullpen was at five, six or seven days off. Being able to spread the load a little bit and not overextend anybody, but also keeping options open if there is a start or something. We want to keep that on the table.
“We were able to do that today and piece it together with four guys instead of just having one guy take on the whole load.”

item.content:encoded:
One miserable inning was enough to put the Red Sox in a hole. A pair of missed opportunities prevented them from climbing out of it.
Patrick Sandoval endured a brutal 44-pitch second inning in which the Rangers scored four times, and the Red Sox repeatedly came up empty with runners on base in a 4-2 loss Tuesday night at Globe Life Field.
Boston (82-69) opened its final road trip of the regular season with a loss and fell to 7-6 in September. The Red Sox did, however, move another step closer to securing a postseason berth after Toronto was routed by Detroit, reducing Boston’s magic number to five.
Any potential celebration will have to wait until after the Red Sox leave Texas. Even if Boston wins the final two games of the series, Toronto is off Thursday and would remain mathematically alive entering Friday.
Sandoval’s night began when he struck out the first four Rangers he faced before everything unraveled in a second inning that seemed as though it might never end.
With two outs, Brandon Nimmo and Ezequiel Duran delivered hard-hit singles at 106.3 mph and 105.3 mph, respectively. Elias Díaz followed by pulling a two-run double into left field to give Texas a 2-0 lead.
Sandoval never recovered walking former Sox catcher Danny Jansen and Justin Foscue before Corey Seager dropped a bloop single into shallow left, just beyond the reach of Trevor Story, allowing two more runs to score. By the time Sandoval finally escaped, he had thrown 44 pitches in the inning and Boston trailed 4-0.
Sandoval lasted just 2 2/3 innings and saw his ERA climb to 4.99.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
The left-hander’s return from injury provided Boston with some needed innings after he was activated July 9, and he delivered several quality outings along the way. But with the postseason approaching, his place on the October roster has become increasingly uncertain.
Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett are ahead of him in the rotation picture, while Brayan Bello has found success in a bulk role. Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck are also attempting to return before the postseason.
Patrick Sandoval strikes out the side in the 1st.
Justin Foscue made him throw 9 pitches to start the game. Needed 19 total to finish the inning. pic.twitter.com/qpUpDLA5Rc
Sandoval will have time to try and clean things up, but it’s looking as if the Red Sox are better suited with the lefty as a spectator when they inevitably travel to the Bronx.
Boston’s offense quickly cut the deficit in half against Jacob deGrom.
Nick Sogard jumped on a pitch in the third and sent it down the right-field line for a two-run homer, pulling the Red Sox within 4-2.
Sogard didn’t hit his first major league homer until his 322nd plate appearance Aug. 19. He has now hit five in his last 99 plate appearances, all coming over a 24-game span.
The versatile infielder contributed in other ways, too. Sogard perfectly executed a sacrifice bunt in the fifth to move two runners into scoring position and later made an athletic play to complete a 1-4-3 double play.
But the Red Sox couldn’t capitalize on their opportunities against deGrom. The Texas right-hander held Boston to three hits and struck out eight over five innings while maintaining a fastball around 97 mph.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Patrick Sandoval allows four runs in second, Red Sox lose opener to Rangers
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: Patrick Sandoval has had a rocky month. item.content:encoded:
Patrick Sandoval has had a rocky month. Entering Tuesday, the Red Sox left-hander had allowed a 6.12 ERA over his last five starts, but coming out of the gate Sandoval looked like he’d finally figured things out.
But after striking out the first four batters he faced, the wheels came off in the bottom of the second.
Sandoval allowed four runs over an interminable 44-pitch second inning and ultimately got the hook after recording just eight outs in Boston’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers.
Nick Sogard hit a two-run home run to help get the Red Sox back into the game, but the offense otherwise couldn’t get anything going against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers bullpen, squandering bases loaded opportunities in the fifth and eighth innings.
Sandoval started strong by striking out the side in the first inning, but after sending down Jake Burger to start the second everything ground to a screeching halt. The right-hander allowed a pair of singles, served up a two-run double to Elias Diaz, and then walked back-to-back batters to load the bases for five-time All-Star Corey Seager.
It appeared for a moment like Sandoval might minimize the damage when he drew a pop fly to shallow left, but the ball drifted into no-man’s land and Trevor Story couldn’t make the catch, allowing two more runs to score and putting the Rangers up 4-0.
Sandoval ultimately needed 44 pitches to get through the second, blowing up his pitch count and ensuring a long evening for the Red Sox bullpen. He recorded two outs in the third and was lifted for Brayan Bello after allowing four runs over 2 2/3 innings.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Arlington postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
Four runs matches the largest deficit the Red Sox have overcome in a win this season, but the club didn’t need long to cut it in half. After Caleb Durbin reached on a one-out single in the top of the third, Sogard ripped a line drive off deGrom that cleared the right field fence for a two-run home run.
It was the fifth home run of the season for Sogard, all of which have come since Aug. 19. Prior to that the 29-year-old had never hit a homer over his first three seasons as a big leaguer.
That wound up being as close as Boston got.
The Red Sox could have tied the score or taken the lead with one swing in the fifth inning, but despite loading the bases without recording a hit the club couldn’t get a run across. Jarren Duran was hit by a pitch, Durbin reached on catcher’s interference and Mickey Gasper walked to bring up Adley Rutschman with two outs, but the catcher grounded out to short to keep it a 4-2 game.
Boston’s bullpen did its part to keep the Red Sox in the game. Bello tossed 1 2/3 perfect innings, Alec Gamboa threw one scoreless aided in large part by a brilliant double play turned by Sogard to end the fifth, and Wyatt Olds worked his way out of a runners-at-the-corners, two-out jam to escape the sixth. Jovani Moran entered with a man on in the seventh and got three quick outs, setting the table for one last Red Sox push in the eighth.
Jahmai Jones sparked the rally with a leadoff single, Willson Contreras drew a one-out walk, and after Wilyer Abreu grounded out to move the two runners into scoring position Story was intentionally walked to load the bases again.
Rather than have Duran face the left-hander Jacob Latz, Tracy pinch hit Andruw Monasterio, but the move didn’t pay off. Monasterio worked a full count and nearly went deep on a hard hit liner that landed just foul before striking out to leave them loaded again.
Boston went quietly in the top of the ninth, finishing the game 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position while stranding nine men on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up and we couldn’t do it tonight,” Tracy said.
Magic number still 5
In addition to keeping pace in the AL West race, the Rangers also jumped the Toronto Blue Jays to become the first team below the AL Wild Card cutline. As a result the Red Sox’s magic number remains five despite the Blue Jays’ 10-1 loss earlier in the night.
Boston (82-69) can clinch a playoff berth as early as Friday, and depending on how things play out in the AL Central the Red Sox could lock down the second Wild Card spot as soon as this weekend.
Houck scoreless with WooSox
Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery rehab) tossed a scoreless inning of relief in his latest rehab appearance with the WooSox on Tuesday. The right-hander entered the game in the seventh inning and allowed one walk, no hits and struck out three over 22 pitches.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox never fully resolved their outfield-designated hitter logjam, and once again it may create a roster conundrum. For much of the season, things had worked themselves out one way or another.
Spending most of the season without Roman Anthony certainly wasn't ideal, but it did make for a cleaner lineup card. His return, of course, has been music to our ears, and it saved the Red Sox from another tough roster decision due to the injuries to Masataka Yoshida and Ceddanne Rafaela.
There's a point where push might come to shove, though, and Boston is forced to make a tough choice. Chad Tracy won't rule out Yoshida returning in time for the playoffs, which would lead to some interesting decisions.
"He's [Yoshida] not on the 60-day (injured list). It's just a matter of how does he heal over the next handful of weeks," the interim skipper said.
If the 33-year-old can return in time for October, it could put the likes of Mickey Gasper or Nick Sogard in the crosshairs. At which point, the Red Sox will have to make a choice and leave someone unhappy.
Masataka Yoshida shouldn't cost Mickey Gasper or Nick Sogard a spot on the Red Sox playoff roster
Just because Yoshida can come back (and that's still up in the air) doesn't mean he should. The NPB veteran has done what he's always done since coming stateside, hit for some average and get on base, but has provided very little in the power department.
Through 87 games, he's hit .274/.347/.399 with five homers, which is nothing to sneeze at, but doesn't really scratch the Red Sox's power itch. On top of that, despite what we saw in the World Baseball Classic, he has little defensive value and will be a nonfactor in the outfield coming off a serious hamstring strain.
Comparatively, Gasper's hot bat better fits what Boston needs. While he might simply be riding the wave rather than emerging as a true offensive force, the switch-hitter has brought the pop with eight dingers in just 187 plate appearances and a .500 slugging percentage, all while providing similar contact and on-base numbers to Yoshida.
Furthermore, he has some value in the field with the ability to fill in behind the plate if needed, as well as play first base. That alone gives him an edge over the DH-only Yoshida.
As for Sogard, his offensive profile is similar to Yoshida's, but his positional versatility is far superior. Depending on Curtis Mead's recovery, Sogard is a valuable insurance policy at second base that should have him over Yoshida in the October pecking order, too.
Craig Breslow's failure to move Jarren Duran before he became a radioactive asset is the real key here. Not only does it represent a missed opportunity for the Red Sox, but it is also the main barrier for Yoshida, given that Boston can't really afford to carry a DH-only player. With that, the choice should be clear. Even if Yoshida is healthy, he needs to sit this October out.

item.content:encoded:
We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.
